title_en: Fragment on the Letter to Philemon
author: Photius of Constantinople
occasion: A brief catena comment on Philemon 1:1, explaining why Paul introduces his appeal for Onesimus by first establishing his own standing (ἀξία), which consists in being in chains (τὸ δεδέσθαι).
argument: Photius observes that in many letters Paul places an unusual word (ξένον ῥῆμα) to prepare for the argument he is about to introduce. Here, because Paul intends to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he makes his request on the basis of his own ἀξία (standing/worth)—and his ἀξία is precisely that he is in chains. By this means he shows the credibility (τὸ ἀξιόπιστον) of his appeal/entreaty (παρακλήσεως).

outline.move: Photius explains that Paul often uses an unusual preparatory word; here, because he intends to make a request on behalf of Onesimus on the basis of his own ἀξία (which is his imprisonment), he thereby shows the credibility of his appeal.

_unresolved_facts.claim: explaining why Paul introduces his appeal for Onesimus by first establishing his own standing (ἀξία), which consists in being in chains (τὸ δεδέσθαι)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The fragment does not say Paul first establishes his own standing. It says Paul uses an unusual preparatory word (ξένον ῥῆμα), and here because he intended to make a request (ἀξιοῦν) on behalf of Onesimus on the basis of his own ἀξία—which is being in chains—he shows the credibility of his appeal. The ἀξία is the basis (instrumental dative τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ) for the request, not something established beforehand.
